label: main:embedding
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main:embedding}
Let $(G,\tau)$ be a non-precompact Hausdorff locally quasi-convex
abelian group. There is an order embedding
\[
  (\mathcal P(\mathfrak c),\subseteq)\longrightarrow\mathcal C(G,\tau)
\]
whose image lies in the interval
$[\sigma(G,\widehat G),\tau]$.
head: environment

label: main:cardinalities
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{main:cardinalities}
Every infinite discrete abelian group $D$ satisfies
\[
  |\mathcal C(D)|=\operatorname{width}\mathcal C(D)=2^{2^{|D|}}.
\]
Let $G=\mathbb R^n\times L$ be a locally compact abelian group, where
$L$ has a compact open subgroup $K$, and put
$D=\mathbb Z^n\times(L/K)$. Then
\[
  |\mathcal C(G)|=\operatorname{width}\mathcal C(G)=
  \begin{cases}
    1,&G\text{ is compact},\\
    2^{2^{|D|}},&G\text{ is non-compact}.
  \end{cases}
\]
For non-compact $\sigma$-compact $G$, both invariants equal
$2^{\mathfrak c}$.
head: environment

label: prop:uniform-basic
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:uniform-basic}
Let $(G,\tau)$ be a topological abelian group and let
$S,T\subseteq\widehat G$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] The function $q_S$ is symmetric and subadditive.
The topology $\tau_S$ is a group topology with a quasi-convex
zero-neighborhood base. Every $\chi\in S$ is
$\tau_S$-continuous, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-polar}
  V(S,k)=\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^k jS\right)^{\triangleleft},
  \qquad jS=\{j\chi:\chi\in S\}.
\end{equation}
\item[(b)] If $S$ is $\tau$-equicontinuous, then $\tau_S\le\tau$.
\item[(c)] We have
\[
  q_{S\cup T}=\max\{q_S,q_T\},\qquad
  \tau_{S\cup T}=\tau_S\vee\tau_T.
\]
The join identity extends to finite unions.
\item[(d)] If $S$ is finite, $\tau_S$ is the initial topology
determined by the characters in $S$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) Symmetry and subadditivity of $q_S$ follow from the norm on
$\mathbb T$. They give
\[
  -V(S,k)=V(S,k),\qquad
  V(S,2k)+V(S,2k)\subseteq V(S,k).
\]
Thus the decreasing family $\{V(S,k):k\ge1\}$ defines a group
topology. Each $\chi\in S$ is continuous because
$\left\|\chi(x)\right\|\le q_S(x)$. By \eqref{eq:small-arcs},
$V(S,k)$ is the inverse polar in \eqref{eq:uniform-polar},
hence quasi-convex.

(b) Equicontinuity makes every $V(S,k)$ a
$\tau$-zero-neighborhood, so $\tau_S\le\tau$.

(c) The maximum identity follows from the definition of $q_S$.
It gives $V(S\cup T,k)=V(S,k)\cap V(T,k)$, proving the join
identity.

(d) For finite $S$, the sets
$V(S,k)=\bigcap_{\chi\in S}\{x:\left\|\chi(x)\right\|\le1/(4k)\}$
form a neighborhood base for the initial topology.
head: environment

label: prop:uniform-joins
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:uniform-joins}
Let $(G,\tau)$ be a Hausdorff locally quasi-convex abelian group,
put $\sigma=\sigma(G,\widehat G)$, and let
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal P(\widehat G)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] The topology $\tau_{\mathcal S}$ has a quasi-convex
zero-neighborhood base
\[
  V(S_1\cup\cdots\cup S_r,k),\qquad
  S_1,\ldots,S_r\in\mathcal S,\quad k\ge1,
\]
where $r$ is finite and $r=0$ gives $G$.
\item[(b)] The Bohr topology is
\[
  \sigma=\bigvee_{\substack{F\subseteq\widehat G\\F\text{ finite}}}
    \tau_F.
\]
Thus adjoining all finite subsets of $\widehat G$ to
$\mathcal S$ gives $\sigma\vee\tau_{\mathcal S}$.
\item[(c)] If every $S\in\mathcal S$ is $\tau$-equicontinuous,
then
\[
  \nu=\sigma\vee\tau_{\mathcal S}\in\mathcal C(G,\tau).
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a) A basic neighborhood in the join is a finite intersection
of sets $V(S_i,k_i)$. For $r\ge1$, taking $k=\max_i k_i$ gives
the smaller quasi-convex neighborhood
\[
  \bigcap_{i=1}^r V(S_i,k)=V(S_1\cup\cdots\cup S_r,k).
\]
The empty intersection gives $G$.

(b) This follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform-basic}(d)
and the definition of $\sigma$.

(c) Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform-basic}(b) gives
$\sigma\le\nu\le\tau$. By (a)--(b), $\nu$ is locally
quasi-convex. It is Hausdorff because $\sigma$ is Hausdorff
and $\sigma\le\nu$; \eqref{eq:sandwich} gives compatibility.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The finite-union identity in
Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform-basic}(c) need not hold for infinite unions.
For example, let $G=\mathbb T^\mathbb N$ have its product topology and put
$S=\{\pi_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$, where $\pi_n$ is the $n$th coordinate
character. Then $\bigvee_n\tau_{\{\pi_n\}}$ is the product
topology, whereas $\tau_S$ is strictly finer: $V(S,1)$ contains
no product zero-neighborhood. Also, $\tau_S$ alone need not be
compatible with $\tau$; Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform-joins}(c)
is the compatibility statement used below.
head: environment

label: lem:finite-equicont
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:finite-equicont}
Every equicontinuous family of characters of a precompact abelian
group is finite. Thus, if $P$ is precompact and
$M\subseteq\widehat P$ is infinite, then for every
zero-neighborhood $V$ in $P$ there exist $f\in M$ and $x\in V$
such that $\left\|f(x)\right\|>1/4$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $M$ be equicontinuous. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a
zero-neighborhood $V$ such that
$\left\|f(v)\right\|<\varepsilon/4$ for all $f\in M$ and $v\in V$.
Precompactness gives a finite set of centers
$x_1,\ldots,x_r$ with $P=\bigcup_{i=1}^r(x_i+V)$.
Equip $M$ with the uniform metric
\[
  d_\infty(f,g)=\sup_{x\in P}\left\|f(x)-g(x)\right\|.
\]
The evaluation vectors $(f(x_i))_{i=1}^r$, $f\in M$, lie in the
compact metric space $\mathbb T^r$, whose metric is
$d_r(z,w)=\max_{1\le i\le r}\left\|z_i-w_i\right\|$.
Consequently, there are finitely many characters
$g_1,\ldots,g_s\in M$ such that for every $f\in M$ there is a $k$
with
\[
  \max_{1\le i\le r}\left\|f(x_i)-g_k(x_i)\right\|<\varepsilon/4.
\]
Fix such $f$ and $k$. Every $x\in P$ has a representation
$x=x_i+v$ with $v\in V$, and hence
\[
  \left\|f(x)-g_k(x)\right\|
  \le\left\|f(x_i)-g_k(x_i)\right\|+\left\|f(v)\right\|+\left\|g_k(v)\right\|
  <3\varepsilon/4.
\]
Thus $d_\infty(f,g_k)\le3\varepsilon/4<\varepsilon$.
The finite family $\{g_1,\ldots,g_s\}$ is therefore an
$\varepsilon$-net for $M$ in the uniform metric. Since
$\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $M$ is totally bounded.

If $f\ne g$, the image of $f-g$ is a nonzero subgroup of $\mathbb T$.
Every such subgroup contains an element of norm at least $1/3$.
Indeed, choose a nonzero element, change its sign if necessary,
and represent it by $a\in(0,1/2]$. If $a<1/3$, the least positive
integer $n$ with $na\ge1/3$ satisfies $1/3\le na<2/3$, so
$\left\|na+\mathbb Z\right\|\ge1/3$; if $a\ge1/3$, the chosen element already
has the required norm. Consequently,
\[
  f\ne g\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_\infty(f,g)\ge1/3.
\]
Now take a finite $1/4$-net $\{g_1,\ldots,g_s\}\subseteq M$ as
above. For each $f\in M$, the inequality
$d_\infty(f,g_k)<1/4$ for some $k$ forces $f=g_k$.
Thus $M=\{g_1,\ldots,g_s\}$ is finite.

For the second assertion, suppose instead that
$f(V)\subseteq\mathbb T_+$ for every $f\in M$. The zero-neighborhoods
$V_m=\bigcap_{j=1}^m j_P^{-1}(V)$ then satisfy
$\left\|f(x)\right\|\le1/(4m)$ for all $f\in M$ and $x\in V_m$, by
\eqref{eq:small-arcs}. This would make $M$ equicontinuous and
hence finite, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:infinite-polar
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:infinite-polar}
Every non-precompact locally quasi-convex group $(G,\tau)$ has a
quasi-convex zero-neighborhood $U$ whose polar $E=U^{\triangleright}$ is
infinite, equicontinuous, and compact for pointwise convergence
on $G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a zero-neighborhood having no finite covering by translates,
and choose a quasi-convex zero-neighborhood $U$ contained in it.
No finite collection of translates of $U$ covers $G$.

Work in the compact product $\mathbb T^G$, whose induced topology on a
family of functions is the topology of pointwise convergence.
For $x\in G$, the evaluation map $e_x:\mathbb T^G\to\mathbb T$, given by
$e_x(p)=p(x)$, is continuous. The set of abstract homomorphisms is
\[
  \operatorname{Hom}(G,\mathbb T)=\bigcap_{x,y\in G}
  \{p\in\mathbb T^G:p(x+y)-p(x)-p(y)=0\}.
\]
Each set in this intersection is closed, since
$p\mapsto p(x+y)-p(x)-p(y)$ is continuous and $\{0\}$ is closed
in $\mathbb T$. Thus $\operatorname{Hom}(G,\mathbb T)$ is closed in $\mathbb T^G$.
Now put
\[
  K_U=\operatorname{Hom}(G,\mathbb T)\cap\bigcap_{u\in U}e_u^{-1}(\mathbb T_+).
\]
Since $\mathbb T_+$ is closed in $\mathbb T$, each $e_u^{-1}(\mathbb T_+)$ is closed.
Consequently, $K_U$ is closed in $\mathbb T^G$ and hence compact.

It remains to identify $K_U$ with $E=U^{\triangleright}$. For every $m\ge1$,
the set $U_m=\bigcap_{j=1}^mj_G^{-1}(U)$ is a
$\tau$-zero-neighborhood. If $h\in K_U$ and $x\in U_m$, then
$jh(x)=h(jx)\in\mathbb T_+$ for $1\le j\le m$, so
\eqref{eq:small-arcs} gives $\left\|h(x)\right\|\le1/(4m)$.
These estimates prove that every $h\in K_U$ is $\tau$-continuous,
and they hold uniformly for all $h\in K_U$. Thus
$K_U\subseteq\widehat G$, $K_U=E$, and $E$ is equicontinuous.
The equality $E=K_U$ also proves that $E$ is closed in $\mathbb T^G$
and compact for pointwise convergence.

If $E$ were finite, quasi-convexity would imply $U=E^{\triangleleft}$.
This set contains a Bohr zero-neighborhood determined by the
finitely many characters in $E$. Precompactness of the Bohr
topology would then give a finite covering of $G$ by translates
of $U$, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:powerset-chain
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:powerset-chain}
For every infinite cardinal $\kappa$, the poset
$(\mathcal P(\kappa),\subseteq)$ contains a chain of cardinality
$\kappa^+$. In particular, $(\mathcal P(\mathfrak c),\subseteq)$ contains
a chain of cardinality $\mathfrak c^+$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Regard cardinals as initial ordinals. Let $\mu$ be the least
infinite cardinal such that $2^\mu>\kappa$. Cantor's theorem
gives $\mu\le\kappa$. Put
\[
  T=\bigcup_{\alpha<\mu}\{0,1\}^{\alpha},\qquad
  B=\{0,1\}^{\mu}.
\]
Thus $T$ consists of the binary sequences of length less than
$\mu$, and $B$ consists of the branches of length $\mu$.
For every $\alpha<\mu$, we have $2^{|\alpha|}\le\kappa$:
this follows from the minimality of $\mu$ when $\alpha$ is
infinite, and from the infinitude of $\kappa$ when $\alpha$
is finite. Consequently,
\[
  |T|\le\sum_{\alpha<\mu}2^{|\alpha|}
       \le\mu\cdot\kappa=\kappa.
\]

Order $T\cup B$ lexicographically. When a node in $T$ ends,
use a terminal symbol $*$ with $0<*<1$; compare distinct
sequences at the first position where their symbols differ.
For each $b\in B$, define the lower cut
\[
  L_b=\{s\in T:s<b\}.
\]
If $b,c\in B$ and $b<c$, let
\[
  \alpha=\min\{\beta<\mu:b(\beta)\ne c(\beta)\}.
\]
Then $b(\alpha)=0$, $c(\alpha)=1$, and their common prefix
$s=b\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\alpha
  =c\mathbin{\upharpoonright}\alpha\in T$
satisfies $b<s<c$. Hence $L_b\subseteq L_c$ and
$s\in L_c\setminus L_b$, so $L_b\subsetneq L_c$.
It follows that
\[
  \{L_b:b\in B\}\subseteq\mathcal P(T)
\]
is a chain of cardinality $|B|=2^\mu>\kappa$.
Choose an injection $i:T\to\kappa$. The images $i[L_b]$
form a chain in $\mathcal P(\kappa)$ of the same cardinality,
which is at least $\kappa^+$. Selecting $\kappa^+$ members
gives the desired chain. Taking $\kappa=\mathfrak c$ proves the
particular case.
head: environment

label: eq:matrix
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\sigma=\sigma(G,\widehat G)$ and take the infinite compact
equicontinuous set $E$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:infinite-polar}.
An infinite compact Hausdorff space has a non-isolated point;
choose $\chi\in E$ with this property. Put
$\varepsilon_n=2^{-n-6}$ for $n\ge1$.

We first construct $f_n\in E-\chi$ and $x_n\in G$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:matrix}
  \left\|f_n(x_n)\right\|>1/4,\qquad
  \left\|f_j(x_n)\right\|<\varepsilon_n\quad(j\ne n).
\end{equation}
Suppose $f_i,x_i$ have been chosen for $i<n$. The set
\[
  M_n=\{\psi-\chi:\psi\in E,
    \ \left\|(\psi-\chi)(x_i)\right\|<\varepsilon_i\text{ for }i<n\}
\]
is infinite: the conditions on $\psi$ define a relative open
neighborhood of the non-isolated point $\chi$ in the Hausdorff
space $E$, and every such neighborhood is infinite. Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:finite-equicont} to the precompact group
$(G,\sigma)$, the infinite family $M_n$, and the neighborhood
\[
  V_n=\{x\in G:\left\|f_i(x)\right\|<\varepsilon_n\text{ for }i<n\}.
\]
Every member of $M_n$ is a $\sigma$-continuous character. The lemma
gives $f_n\in M_n$ and $x_n\in V_n$ with
$\left\|f_n(x_n)\right\|>1/4$. The definition of $M_n$ controls the new
character at the earlier points, while the definition of $V_n$
controls the earlier characters at the new point. After completing
the recursion, \eqref{eq:matrix} holds for all indices.

For $A\subseteq\mathbb N$, put $S_A=\{f_n:n\in A\}$. Let $\tau_A$
be the topology on $G$ of uniform convergence with respect to
the character family $S_A$.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform-basic}, it has the quasi-convex
zero-neighborhood base
\[
  V(A,k)=\{x\in G:\left\|f_j(x)\right\|\le1/(4k)
    \text{ for every }j\in A\},\qquad k\ge1.
\]
The topology $\tau_A$ need not be Hausdorff. Since $E-\chi$ is
$\tau$-equicontinuous, part (b) of that proposition gives
$\tau_A\le\tau$.

Fix an almost disjoint family
$\{A_\xi:\xi<\mathfrak c\}\subseteq[\mathbb N]^\omega$; thus each $A_\xi$
is infinite and $A_\xi\cap A_\zeta$ is finite for $\xi\ne\zeta$.
Such a family is obtained from the sets of initial segments of
the infinite branches of the countable binary tree. For
$J\subseteq\mathfrak c$, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nuJ}
  \nu_J=\sigma\vee\bigvee_{\xi\in J}\tau_{A_\xi}.
\end{equation}
In the notation for $\mathcal S$-topologies, this is
$\nu_J=\tau_{\mathcal S_J}$, where
\[
  \mathcal S_J=[\widehat G]^{<\omega}
      \cup\{S_{A_\xi}:\xi\in J\},
\]
and $[\widehat G]^{<\omega}$ is the family of all finite subsets
of $\widehat G$. Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform-joins}(b)--(c)
gives $\sigma\le\nu_J\le\tau$ and
$\nu_J\in\mathcal C(G,\tau)$.

For each $\xi<\mathfrak c$, let $W_\xi=V(A_\xi,2)$. We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:membership-test}
  W_\xi\text{ is a }\nu_J\text{-zero-neighborhood}
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\xi\in J.
\end{equation}
If $\xi\in J$, this is immediate from \eqref{eq:nuJ}.
Suppose $\xi\notin J$. A $\nu_J$-zero-neighborhood base consists
of the sets
\[
  B(A,F,\eta)=\{x\in G:\left\|\phi(x)\right\|\le\eta
    \text{ for every }\phi\in S_A\cup F\},
\]
where $F\subseteq\widehat G$ is finite, $\eta>0$, and
$A=\bigcup_{\zeta\in J_0}A_\zeta$ for a finite $J_0\subseteq J$.
Indeed, Proposition~\ref{prop:uniform-joins}(a) allows us to
combine the finitely many character sets involved and use a
smaller common bound. Empty $F$ and $J_0$ are allowed.

Almost disjointness implies that $A_\xi\setminus A$ is infinite.
Restrict to an infinite tail on which $\varepsilon_n<\eta/2$.
Compactness gives a finite cover of $\mathbb T^F$ by sets on each of
which every coordinate varies by less than $\eta$. Since the
tail is infinite, there are distinct indices $n,m$ whose
evaluation vectors $(\psi(x_n))_{\psi\in F}$ and
$(\psi(x_m))_{\psi\in F}$ belong to the same member of this cover.
Hence
\[
  \left\|\psi(x_n)-\psi(x_m)\right\|<\eta\qquad(\psi\in F).
\]
For every $j\in A$, we have $j\ne n,m$, so \eqref{eq:matrix} gives
\[
  \left\|f_j(x_n-x_m)\right\|
  \le\left\|f_j(x_n)\right\|+\left\|f_j(x_m)\right\|
  <\varepsilon_n+\varepsilon_m<\eta.
\]
Thus $x_n-x_m\in B(A,F,\eta)$. On the other hand,
\[
  \left\|f_n(x_n-x_m)\right\|
  \ge\left\|f_n(x_n)\right\|-\left\|f_n(x_m)\right\|
  >1/4-\varepsilon_m>1/8.
\]
Since $n\in A_\xi$, this gives $x_n-x_m\notin W_\xi$.
Thus no basic $\nu_J$-zero-neighborhood is contained in $W_\xi$,
proving \eqref{eq:membership-test}.

The assignment $J\mapsto\nu_J$ is order-preserving. If
$\nu_J\le\nu_{J'}$, every $\nu_J$-neighborhood is also a
$\nu_{J'}$-neighborhood. Applying \eqref{eq:membership-test} to
$W_\xi$ for each $\xi\in J$ gives $J\subseteq J'$. Consequently,
\[
  \nu_J\le\nu_{J'}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad J\subseteq J'.
\]
If $J\subsetneq J'$, choose $\xi\in J'\setminus J$.
Then $W_\xi$ is a $\nu_{J'}$-zero-neighborhood but not a
$\nu_J$-zero-neighborhood, so $\nu_J<\nu_{J'}$.
Thus strict inclusion, equality, and incomparability of indexing
sets correspond exactly to the respective relations between the
associated topologies. The assignment is an order embedding.
head: environment

label: cor:width
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:width}
Every non-precompact Hausdorff locally quasi-convex abelian group
$G$ satisfies
\[
  |\mathcal C(G)|\ge\operatorname{width}\mathcal C(G)\ge2^{\mathfrak c},
\]
and $\mathcal C(G)$ contains a chain of cardinality $\mathfrak c^+$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Partition a set of cardinality $\mathfrak c$ into two-element blocks.
The subsets choosing exactly one element from each block form
an antichain in its power set of cardinality $2^{\mathfrak c}$.
Theorem~\ref{main:embedding} transfers this antichain to $\mathcal C(G)$.
For the chain assertion, Lemma~\ref{lem:powerset-chain} gives
a chain of cardinality $\mathfrak c^+$ in $\mathcal P(\mathfrak c)$, whose image
under the order embedding in Theorem~\ref{main:embedding}
is a chain of the same cardinality in $\mathcal C(G)$.
head: environment

label: cor:universality
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:universality}
If $G$ is a non-precompact Hausdorff locally quasi-convex abelian
group, every poset of cardinality at most $\mathfrak c$ order-embeds into
$[\sigma(G,\widehat G),\tau]\subseteq\mathcal C(G,\tau)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a poset $P$, the map $p\mapsto\{q\in P:q\le p\}$ is an order
embedding into $\mathcal P(P)$. If $|P|\le\mathfrak c$, compose it with an
embedding into $\mathcal P(\mathfrak c)$ and with Theorem~\ref{main:embedding}.
head: environment

label: cor:dichotomy
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:dichotomy}
For every Hausdorff locally quasi-convex abelian group $G$, either
$|\mathcal C(G)|=1$ or $\operatorname{width}\mathcal C(G)\ge2^{\mathfrak c}$.
Consequently, $\mathcal C(G)$ is a chain if and only if it is a singleton.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Bohr topology is the unique precompact member of $\mathcal C(G)$.
If there is another member $\nu$, apply
Theorem~\ref{main:embedding} to $(G,\nu)$ and observe that
$\mathcal C(G,\nu)=\mathcal C(G)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Corollary~\ref{cor:dichotomy} strengthens the conclusion proposed
in \cite[Conjecture 7.6]{ADMP15} and rules out the finite
non-singleton possibility asked about in
\cite[Question 7.5]{ADMP15}. It also answers the chain question
recorded in \cite[Question 1.1(b)]{AD20} for Hausdorff locally
quasi-convex abelian groups.
head: environment

label: thm:discrete
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A finite group has only one Hausdorff topology. If $D$ is
countably infinite, its discrete topology is non-precompact.
Corollary~\ref{cor:width} gives an antichain of size $2^{\mathfrak c}$,
while the number of topologies on a countable set is at most
$|\mathcal P(\mathcal P(D))|=2^{\mathfrak c}$. This proves both equalities.

If $D$ is uncountable, then $\operatorname{r}(D)$ is infinite. To see this,
suppose instead that the displayed rank is finite and put
$T=t(D)$, the torsion subgroup. For each prime $p$, the group
$T[p]$ is finite. Multiplication by $p$ maps $T[p^k]$ into
$T[p^{k-1}]$ with kernel $T[p]$, so induction shows that every
$T[p^k]$ is finite. Each primary component of $T$ is countable,
and there are only countably many primes; hence $T$ is countable.
The torsion-free quotient $D/T$ embeds in a finite-dimensional
rational vector space and is also countable. Thus $D$ is a
countable union of countable cosets and would be countable. The
infinite-rank formula \eqref{eq:infinite-rank} now applies.
head: environment

label: thm:lca
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:lca}
Let $G=\mathbb R^n\times L$ be locally compact abelian, let $K\le L$
be compact and open, and put $D=\mathbb Z^n\times(L/K)$. Then
\[
  |\mathcal C(G)|=\operatorname{width}\mathcal C(G)=
  \begin{cases}
    1,&G\text{ is compact},\\
    2^{2^{|D|}},&G\text{ is non-compact}.
  \end{cases}
\]
If $G$ is non-compact and $\sigma$-compact, then
$|\mathcal C(G)|=\operatorname{width}\mathcal C(G)=2^{\mathfrak c}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Use \eqref{eq:discrete-reduction} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete}. The group $D$ is finite precisely
when $n=0$ and $L/K$ is finite, which is equivalent to compactness
of $G$. If $G$ is $\sigma$-compact, so is $L$, and its discrete
quotient $L/K$ is countable: every compact subset has finite
image in the quotient. Thus $D$ is countably infinite when
$G$ is also non-compact.
head: environment

label: cor:basic-groups
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Each group in the statement is countably infinite and discrete.
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete}.
head: environment

label: cor:finite-products
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:finite-products}
Let $G,G_1,G_2$ be locally compact abelian groups and let $m\ge1$
be an integer. Then
\[
  |\mathcal C(G^m)|=|\mathcal C(G)|,
  \qquad
  |\mathcal C(G_1\times G_2)|
    =\max\{|\mathcal C(G_1)|,|\mathcal C(G_2)|\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose discrete reductions $D,D_1,D_2$ as in
\eqref{eq:discrete-reduction}. The same construction gives
\[
  \mathcal C(G^m)\cong\mathcal C(D^m),\qquad
  \mathcal C(G_1\times G_2)\cong\mathcal C(D_1\times D_2).
\]
For finite $D$, both $D$ and $D^m$ have singleton compatible
posets. For infinite $D$, $|D^m|=|D|$, so the first equality
follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:discrete}. If both $D_i$ are finite,
all three cardinalities in the second equality are $1$.
Otherwise, $|D_1\times D_2|=\max\{|D_1|,|D_2|\}$, and the
same theorem gives the second equality.
head: environment

label: thm:complete
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:complete}
Let $G$ be a non-compact complete metrizable locally quasi-convex
abelian group. Then $\mathcal P(\mathfrak c)$ order-embeds in $\mathcal C(G)$.
Consequently,
\[
  |\mathcal C(G)|\ge\operatorname{width}\mathcal C(G)\ge2^{\mathfrak c},
\]
and $\mathcal C(G)$ contains a chain of cardinality $\mathfrak c^+$.
If $G$ is also separable, then
$|\mathcal C(G)|=\operatorname{width}\mathcal C(G)=2^{\mathfrak c}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A complete precompact group is compact. Hence $G$ is
non-precompact, and Theorem~\ref{main:embedding} and
Corollary~\ref{cor:width} give the embedding, the lower bound,
and the chain.

By the Mackey theorem for complete metrizable locally
quasi-convex groups \cite[Theorem 4.2]{CMT99}, every compatible locally
quasi-convex topology is coarser than the original topology
$\tau$. If $G$ is separable and metrizable, $\tau$ has a
countable base and $|\tau|\le\mathfrak c$. Therefore
\[
  |\mathcal C(G)|\le|\mathcal P(\tau)|\le2^{\mathfrak c}.
\]
The antichain lower bound proves the final assertion.
head: environment

label: prop:nuclear-singleton
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:nuclear-singleton}
Give
\[
  E=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathbb Z(2)
    \subseteq K=\prod_{n\ge1}\mathbb Z(2)
\]
the subspace topology $\tau$ inherited from $K$. Then $E$ is
a non-compact metrizable nuclear group and $\mathcal C(E)=\{\tau\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The subgroup $E$ is proper and dense in $K$, so it is precompact.
If it were compact, it would be closed in the Hausdorff group
$K$, contradicting proper density. It is metrizable and nuclear.

Every continuous character of $E$ extends uniquely to its compact
completion $K$. A continuous character of $K$ depends on finitely
many coordinates. Consequently,
\[
  \widehat E\cong\bigoplus_{n\ge1}\mathbb Z(2)
\]
is countable, and the coordinate characters show that
$\tau=\sigma(E,\widehat E)$.

Let $\nu\in\mathcal C(E)$. A character of a group of exponent two takes
values in $\{0,1/2+\mathbb Z\}$, whose intersection with $\mathbb T_+$ is
$\{0\}$. Hence every quasi-convex subset of $E$ is an intersection
of character kernels and is a subgroup. The topology $\nu$
therefore has a zero-neighborhood base of open subgroups.

If a subgroup $U$ in this base had infinite index, $E/U$ would
be a countably infinite-dimensional $\mathbb F_2$-vector space. Its full
character group has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}=\mathfrak c$. Pullback
along the continuous quotient map from $(E,\nu)$ to the discrete
group $E/U$ would inject this character group into
$(E,\nu)^\wedge=\widehat E$, contradicting countability.

Thus every subgroup $U$ in the base has finite index. The
characters of the finite quotient $E/U$ separate its points,
so $U$ is an intersection of finitely many kernels of
$\nu$-continuous characters. Compatibility makes these
characters $\tau$-continuous, whence $U$ is $\tau$-open.
It follows that $\nu\le\tau$. Conversely,
$\tau=\sigma(E,\widehat E)\le\nu$, so $\nu=\tau$.

label: lem:discrete-top-compact
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The topology $\delta$ is the greatest element because it is
discrete. Every nonempty join of members of $\mathcal C(D)$ is
Hausdorff and locally quasi-convex, and lies between the Bohr
topology and $\delta$. It is therefore compatible, so joins of
topologies compute suprema in $\mathcal C(D)$.

Suppose a nonempty directed family $\{\mu_i:i\in I\}$ has
supremum $\delta$. Since $\{0\}$ is a neighborhood in the join,
there are finitely many indices $i_1,\ldots,i_r$ and
$\mu_{i_j}$-zero-neighborhoods $U_j$ such that
$U_1\cap\cdots\cap U_r\subseteq\{0\}$. Directedness provides
$i\in I$ with $\mu_{i_j}\le\mu_i$ for every $j$. Thus $\{0\}$
is a $\mu_i$-neighborhood and $\mu_i=\delta$. If $D$ is trivial,
the assertion follows immediately.
head: environment

label: prop:no-discrete-reduction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:no-discrete-reduction}
Let $G=\mathbb R^\mathbb N$ have its product topology. Then $G$ is complete
metrizable and nuclear, and
\[
  \mathcal C(G)\not\cong\mathcal C(D)
  \quad\text{for every discrete abelian group }D.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\tau$ be the product topology and
$\sigma=\sigma(G,\widehat G)$. The group $G$ is locally
quasi-convex, complete, and metrizable. Its original topology
$\tau$ is therefore the greatest member of $\mathcal C(G)$ by
\cite[Theorem 4.2]{CMT99}. For $n\ge1$, put
\[
  \nu_n=\sigma\vee\pi_{\le n}^{-1}(\tau_{\mathbb R^n}),
\]
where $\pi_{\le n}$ is the projection onto the first $n$
coordinates. Here the inverse-image topology is allowed to be
non-Hausdorff before taking the join. It is locally quasi-convex,
and $\sigma\le\nu_n\le\tau$, so $\nu_n\in\mathcal C(G)$.

On the $(n+1)$-st coordinate axis, the topology induced by
$\nu_n$ is the Bohr topology of $\mathbb R$. Indeed, the
finite-coordinate topology induces the indiscrete topology
on that axis, and the restrictions of the characters of $G$
give exactly the continuous characters of $\mathbb R$: each such
character extends by composition with the coordinate projection.
The Bohr topology is strictly coarser than the usual topology,
since the former is precompact and the latter is not.
Consequently, $\nu_n<\tau$ for every $n$.

The family $(\nu_n)$ is increasing. Its topological join is
$\tau$, because the usual topologies on finite sets of
coordinates generate the product topology. Hence its supremum
in $\mathcal C(G)$ is $\tau$. This shows that $\tau$ is not
order-compact, whereas the greatest element of every $\mathcal C(D)$
is order-compact by Lemma~\ref{lem:discrete-top-compact}.
The posets cannot be order-isomorphic. Finally, $G$ is nuclear
as a product of locally compact abelian groups.
head: environment
